finding.claim: /fetch2 sends an attacker-supplied URL to requests.get. The only check is that the scheme is http or https, so the server will fetch internal hosts, loopback, and cloud metadata endpoints such as 169.254.169.254. The first 200 characters of the response are returned to the caller, so this is not blind SSRF. Redirects are followed, so a public URL can redirect to an internal address.
finding.sink: views.py:22 requests.get(url, timeout=5).text[:200] returned in the JSON response

trace.note: url taken from request.args, fully attacker-controlled
is_http_url returns urlparse(url).scheme in ('http','https'); it does not inspect hostname or resolved IP
requests.get(url, timeout=5) with default allow_redirects=True; response text returned to attacker

finding.guards_checked: is_http_url (validators.py:6-7): scheme allowlist only. No hostname, IP-range, port, or redirect-target checks. Not a meaningful SSRF defense. Fix: apply an is_safe_url-style IP check, pin the resolved IP, and disable redirects or re-validate each hop.

verdict.guard_found: None on the /fetch2 path. views.py:20 calls is_http_url, which validators.py:7 implements as a scheme-only check (urlparse(url).scheme in ("http","https")) with no hostname, IP, or redirect checks. The stronger is_safe_url (validators.py:10-18) is used only by /fetch at views.py:12, not /fetch2. views.py:22 uses default allow_redirects=True and returns .text[:200] to the caller.
verdict.reason: The source is request.args at views.py:19, which is attacker-controlled; the only guard, is_http_url at views.py:20 and validators.py:7, is scheme-only, so requests.get at views.py:22 will fetch internal, loopback, and metadata addresses and return the first 200 characters of the response. The candidate's trace is accurate; the sibling /fetch route at views.py:12-14 shows the intended defense (is_safe_url, redirects disabled) was not applied to /fetch2.

finding.claim: /fetch validates the URL with is_safe_url, but the validation and the fetch resolve DNS separately (time-of-check/time-of-use). An attacker-controlled hostname with a short TTL can return a public IP during validation and then 127.0.0.1 or an RFC1918 address when requests.get resolves it again (DNS rebinding). Impact depends on attacker-controlled DNS and the rebinding window. The private-range list may also have gaps (see guards_checked), which I could not confirm by running code.
finding.sink: views.py:14 requests.get(url, timeout=5, allow_redirects=False).text[:200] returned in the JSON response

trace.note: scheme must be http or https and hostname must be present
socket.getaddrinfo(hostname) resolves DNS; this is the check-time resolution
rejects is_private, is_loopback, is_link_local, is_reserved for every returned address
requests.get(url) resolves the hostname again at fetch time; the IP is not pinned, so the second lookup can return a different address

finding.guards_checked: Scheme allowlist; hostname required; all resolved IPs checked against is_private/is_loopback/is_link_local/is_reserved; allow_redirects=False blocks redirect-based bypass. Not covered: DNS rebinding (no IP pinning between check and use). Possible gap, unconfirmed: 100.64.0.0/10 (CGNAT, which includes Alibaba metadata 100.100.100.200) and IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses may not be flagged by these checks depending on the Python version. I could not run the check because the shell command was not approved.

verdict.guard_found: none closing. views.py:12 is_safe_url(url) and validators.py:12-18 (scheme check, hostname required, resolved-IP private/loopback/link-local/reserved check) are not one of the accepted closing guards, and nothing pins the resolved IP between check and use at views.py:14. views.py:14 allow_redirects=False blocks redirects only, not rebinding.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: url comes from request.args (views.py:11), is checked by is_safe_url (views.py:12, validators.py:14-18) which resolves DNS once, and requests.get(url) (views.py:14) resolves the hostname again with no IP pinning, so an attacker-controlled DNS name can rebind from a public to a private address; this is a real but timing- and DNS-dependent SSRF. The candidate's unconfirmed concern about 100.64.0.0/10 and IPv4-mapped IPv6 is not needed for this verdict and is not verified. Separately, views.py:22 (/fetch2) fetches the same kind of URL with only the scheme check, which is a stronger finding than the one under review.
